paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Matrix multiplication takes two matrices and builds a third matrix out of them. It only works when the first matrix has exactly as many columns as the second one has rows. The answer, called the matrix product, has as many rows as the first matrix and as many columns as the second. The product of A and B is written simply as AB.

paragraphs.heading: How each entry is found
paragraphs.text: To fill in the entry in row i and column j of the product, take row i of A and column j of B. Multiply their entries in matching pairs, then add all of those products together. In other words, that entry is the dot product of the row with the column. This is why AB exists only when A has as many columns as B has rows.

paragraphs.heading: Order matters
paragraphs.text: Matrix multiplication behaves like ordinary multiplication in some ways, but not in all of them. An operation is called commutative when swapping the two factors always gives the same result. Matrix multiplication is not commutative: AB and BA can differ even when both of them make sense. One case where the order stops mattering is when D and E are square diagonal matrices of the same size, so that DE = ED.

paragraphs.heading: Where it came from
paragraphs.text: The French mathematician Jacques Philippe Marie Binet first described the operation in 1812. He used it to stand for the composition of linear maps that are written as matrices. It was brought in to make the calculations of linear algebra easier and clearer. Today, computing matrix products sits at the centre of every computer application of linear algebra, and the tool turns up in statistics, physics, economics and engineering.

paragraphs.heading: A factory example
paragraphs.text: Picture a factory. One matrix, A, records how many units of each basic commodity go into each intermediate good. A second matrix, B, records how many intermediate goods go into each final product. Their product AB tells you directly how much of each basic commodity a final product needs. Its bottom left entry works out as 1⋅1 + 1⋅2 + 2⋅4 = 11, so 11 units of the commodity b₄ go into one unit of the final good f₁.

paragraphs.heading: Vectors as thin matrices
paragraphs.text: A vector with n components can be treated as a matrix with a single row or a single column. Seen this way, the dot product of two column vectors a and b is the lone entry of the 1 × 1 matrix 𝐚^T𝐛, a row times a column. Multiplying the other way round, a column times a row, gives the outer product 𝐚𝐛^T, which is a full n × n matrix.
